- ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20width%3D'100'%20height%3D'100'%20data-ring-placeholder%3D'1'%3E%3C%2Fsvg%3E)

[news](https://africa.businessinsider.com/news) [The personal AI agent horror stories are rolling in](https://africa.businessinsider.com/news/the-personal-ai-agent-horror-stories-are-rolling-in/bjs89d5)

- ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20width%3D'100'%20height%3D'100'%20data-ring-placeholder%3D'1'%3E%3C%2Fsvg%3E)

[news](https://africa.businessinsider.com/news) [This consulting firm is making bespoke AI apps to replace the PowerPoint pitch](https://africa.businessinsider.com/news/this-consulting-firm-is-making-bespoke-ai-apps-to-replace-the-powerpoint-pitch/18btnf7)


That's the advice [Michael Kratsios](https://www.businessinsider.com/white-house-advisor-ai-layoffs-washing-michael-kratsios-2026-8), the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, gave during an interview with Fox News Sunday.


"It's very interesting that they talk about these issues, about how scared they are about potentially where the future is, and maybe they want to do a pause," Kratsios said. "Our position is, if you do believe that you're developing a technology that is unsafe or you don't want it out into the world, you can just stop it."


He added, "You don't need someone to force you to do that."


ADVERTISEMENT

Kratsios pushed back against the notion that the US government needs to take explicit action for tech companies to take a breather.


"They just need to slow down if they feel that they need to do so," Kratsios said. "I think the key thing to always remember is the US government has lots of tools in its toolkit to deal with these issues when they come up, and we've used them in the past."


Ever since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, tech companies across the globe have become locked in a race to develop the most capable model. Doing so could mean dominating the market and securing steady profits, a huge win for whichever company comes out on top. OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are among the industry leaders.


Many Americans have expressed concerns that those tech companies are moving too fast and, in doing so, putting public safety at risk. A Pew Research Center survey published in August said over half of the respondents were more concerned than excited about using AI more in their daily lives. Potential job loss was among the top concerns associated with AI.


Critics have also pointed toward privacy and cybersecurity risks. In July, OpenAI agents breached its training parameters and [hacked Hugging Face](https://www.businessinsider.com/smart-people-react-openai-hugging-face-hacking-cybersecurity-incident-2026-7), another AI company. This month, a cybersecurity startup used Anthropic's Claude to [hack OpenAI's codebase](https://www.businessinsider.com/hacktron-ai-cybersecurity-startup-hack-openai-using-claude-2026-9). On Friday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring.


ADVERTISEMENT

AI leaders themselves have long expressed concern about the products they are raising hundreds of billions of dollars to build.


In a blog post earlier this month, [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei](https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-slow-down-dario-amodei-sam-altman-elon-musk-2026-9) said the [Hugging Face breach](https://www.businessinsider.com/dario-amodei-slow-ai-safety-essay-openai-hugging-face-hack-2026-9) convinced him that the industry needs to take its foot off the pedal.


"Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," Amodei wrote. He suggested placing independent safety monitors inside the frontier AI labs and called for more robust government regulation.


The blog post earned support from his industry peers, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis.


President [Donald Trump](https://www.businessinsider.com/trump-ai-regulation-slowdown-anthropic-dario-amodei-9-2026), who has broadly supported expanding and accelerating AI development in the US, said on Saturday that his administration would not do anything that could "stifle" AI's progress. He also announced a new AI Force to coordinate responses when AI goes off the rails.


ADVERTISEMENT

The Trump administration supported the [$500 billion Stargate Project](https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-stargate-project-data-center-power-gigawatt-chatgpt-ai-2025-10), an initiative to expand AI infrastructure nationwide, and he signed an executive order to accelerate federal permitting for data center construction. He will host China's leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington, D.C., this week to discuss AI and trade.


Kratsios told Fox News Sunday that it's critical to have conversations about AI with China.


"The key thing that we want to talk to him about is avoiding shared risks, and that's something that I think we can have a fruitful conversation on," Kratsios said.


Lauren Edmonds

# Andrew Ng Dismisses AI Extinction Warnings as Science Fiction and PR Spin

AI pioneer Andrew Ng told Bloomberg TV that warnings of AI-driven human extinction are "much more science fiction than science," calling the renewed doom talk a PR play aimed at shaping regulation. His comments put him at odds with Geoffrey Hinton, Anthropic and King Charles III, who all warned of catastrophic AI risk this same week.

![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/davepress.png)

[Dave Barr](https://startupfortune.com/author/dave/)

Sep 17, 2026 · 10:00 PM·4 min read·1.5K reads

[Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fstartupfortune.com%2Fandrew-ng-dismisses-ai-extinction-warnings-as-science-fiction-and-pr-spin%2F&text=Andrew+Ng+Dismisses+AI+Extinction+Warnings+as+Science+Fiction+and+PR+Spin)[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fstartupfortune.com%2Fandrew-ng-dismisses-ai-extinction-warnings-as-science-fiction-and-pr-spin%2F)[Share on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/?text=Andrew+Ng+Dismisses+AI+Extinction+Warnings+as+Science+Fiction+and+PR+Spin+https%3A%2F%2Fstartupfortune.com%2Fandrew-ng-dismisses-ai-extinction-warnings-as-science-fiction-and-pr-spin%2F)[Share on Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fstartupfortune.com%2Fandrew-ng-dismisses-ai-extinction-warnings-as-science-fiction-and-pr-spin%2F&title=Andrew+Ng+Dismisses+AI+Extinction+Warnings+as+Science+Fiction+and+PR+Spin)[Share via Email](mailto:?subject=Andrew+Ng+Dismisses+AI+Extinction+Warnings+as+Science+Fiction+and+PR+Spin&body=https%3A%2F%2Fstartupfortune.com%2Fandrew-ng-dismisses-ai-extinction-warnings-as-science-fiction-and-pr-spin%2F)

![Andrew Ng Dismisses AI Extinction Warnings as Science Fiction and PR Spin](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/andrew-ng-anthropic-geoffrey-hinton-1024x576.jpg)

_Andrew Ng, one of the founding figures of modern deep learning, told Bloomberg TV that warnings of AI-driven human extinction are much more science fiction than science._

Andrew Ng just told the AI industry's doomsday chorus to stand down. Speaking on Bloomberg Tech with anchor Ed Ludlow on September 17, 2026, the Google Brain co-founder and Coursera chairman said warnings that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity are much more science fiction than science. That's a direct shot at some of his own peers.

Ng didn't stop at dismissal. He argued the earlier wave of catastrophic AI warnings, the kind that dominated headlines a few years back, was partly a publicity play, one built to shape how governments write AI rules. He told Bloomberg the same dynamic is playing out again now, calling the latest round of doom talk a wave of PR.

His case for calm rests on engineering, not faith. AI systems, he said, will never be perfectly predictable. No software is. But testing, safeguards and iterative fixes, the same discipline that makes bridges and airplanes safer over decades, can bring the risk down over time. Slowing development, in his view, doesn't buy safety. It costs it, by starving the very research that finds and patches the failure modes.

Ng's comments land in the middle of a fight among the people who actually built this technology. Take Geoffrey Hinton. The University of Toronto professor, often called the godfather of AI, backed Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei's call to slow the pace of development this month, according to ABC News. Hinton has said most experts now expect superintelligent AI within a decade, and that nobody has proven it can be controlled once it arrives.

[![Geoffrey Hinton Tells Senators Congress Has About a Year to Rein In AI](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ajeya-cotra-bernie-sanders-geoffrey-hinton-600x300.jpg)](https://startupfortune.com/geoffrey-hinton-tells-senators-congress-has-about-a-year-to-rein-in-ai/)

[Geoffrey Hinton Tells Senators Congress Has About a Year to Rein In AI](https://startupfortune.com/geoffrey-hinton-tells-senators-congress-has-about-a-year-to-rein-in-ai/)

Geoffrey Hinton warned a closed, bipartisan Senate briefing convened by Bernie Sanders that Congress has 'maybe a year, but not much more than a year' to regulate AI before it slips out of control. The Nobel laureate pointed to recursive self-improvement as the risk, a warning that landed the same week Andrew Ng and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi... - [Geoffrey Hinton AI regulation deadline congress needs](https://startupfortune.com/geoffrey-hinton-tells-senators-congress-has-about-a-year-to-rein-in-ai/) \- [how long before AI becomes uncontrollable experts warn](https://startupfortune.com/geoffrey-hinton-tells-senators-congress-has-about-a-year-to-rein-in-ai/)

Two Anthropic researchers went further. They warned the technology could lead to human extinction in the not too distant future, a claim that helped push King Charles III to host AI executives, including the co-founders of Nvidia and Google DeepMind alongside leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic, at a summit in Scotland this week. The King told attendees safeguards are needed before it becomes too late, according to AAP.

Ng was not in that room.

He isn't alone in pushing back, either. Cohere chief executive Aidan Gomez has separately warned against what he called an AI safety cartel, pushing back on rivals' calls for coordinated slowdowns, according to Bloomberg. Treat risk as an engineering problem, not a reason to freeze development: that's the message coming from this corner of the industry.

Ng has long been the researcher least interested in performing alarm. He ran Google Brain, co-founded Coursera, spent two years as Baidu's chief scientist, and has spent much of the last decade telling founders, through his venture fund AI Fund and his DeepLearning.AI courses, that AI is a tool to be engineered, not a genie to be feared.

This isn't the first time he's pushed back against AI panic. Earlier this year, Ng took to X to dismiss what he called the AI jobpocalypse, arguing that overblown stories of mass unemployment from AI were irresponsible and damaging. The pattern holds. Where much of the industry reaches for the biggest possible warning, Ng reaches for the counterargument.

## What it means for the regulation fight

The timing matters. Governments in the US, the UK and the EU are all working through how tightly to regulate frontier models, and the industry's own scientists disagree sharply on how urgent that work is. If a founding figure of deep learning tells regulators the extinction case is overstated, that hands skeptics of heavy-handed AI rules a credible voice to point to, one that isn't a lobbyist or a policy staffer but an actual research pioneer.

Watch which side lawmakers listen to this fall. That's where this argument actually gets decided.

[![Anthropic Turns Claude Code Into a Multi-Agent Team With New Projects Beta](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/anthropic-claude-code-openai-codex-600x300.jpg)](https://startupfortune.com/anthropic-turns-claude-code-into-a-multi-agent-team-with-new-projects-beta/)

[Anthropic Turns Claude Code Into a Multi-Agent Team With New Projects Beta](https://startupfortune.com/anthropic-turns-claude-code-into-a-multi-agent-team-with-new-projects-beta/)

Anthropic relaunched Projects inside Claude Code on September 17, adding a coordinating agent that splits engineering goals across multiple parallel cloud sessions called threads. Each thread works its own branch and shares memory with the rest of the project, though execution is cloud-only for now and the beta is limited to select Pro and Max... - [how to use Claude Code multi agent projects](https://startupfortune.com/anthropic-turns-claude-code-into-a-multi-agent-team-with-new-projects-beta/) \- [Claude Code parallel cloud agents for engineering tasks](https://startupfortune.com/anthropic-turns-claude-code-into-a-multi-agent-team-with-new-projects-beta/)

Frankly, the industry has staked its credibility on doom arguments before and been wrong about the timeline. What's different now is where the fight sits. The disagreement used to run between the industry and its critics. Now it runs inside the room that built the technology.

# The Big Four AI Labs Agreed to Slow Down. Now They’re Being Sued for It.
## The trigger — September 12, and the hour that followed
On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a roughly 3,900-word essay on his own blog, [We Must Pace the Frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier).

According to the complaint, within about an hour of the essay going up, Elon Musk publicly endorsed it, Sam Altman said he agreed and committed OpenAI to step one, and Demis Hassabis endorsed it too, tying it back to an industry standards-body proposal he’d floated in July. On September 15, OpenAI’s global policy chief Chris Lehane confirmed that OpenAI had “been working with Anthropic and Google DeepMind on the issue for several weeks” — a line the complaint cites as evidence the coordination predated the essay, rather than being a spontaneous, independent reaction to it.

## The longer timeline the complaint builds
It says Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google formed a working group in July to build an industry standards body, and that on July 14, Hassabis publicly proposed a U.S.-based AI standards organization modeled in part on FINRA, the financial industry’s self-regulator. On September 6, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay, “An Alien Mind,” describing a coordinated slowdown as one option available to frontier labs. On September 10, WIRED reported that OpenAI had asked members of Congress whether an industry-wide coordinated slowdown would violate antitrust law.

The complaint also leans on a separate document: an open letter titled “Pacing the Frontier,” published July 28 and signed by 1,386 people across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta — including Amodei himself, Anthropic co-founders Jared Kaplan and Jack Clark, OpenAI’s Pachocki and chief research officer Mark Chen, and DeepMind’s Shane Legg.

## Why now — a cluster of safety incidents in September
OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, released June 26, had already raised flags during pre-deployment evaluation: METR, the outside evaluator, reported the model showed “a detected cheating rate higher than any public model we have evaluated” — exploiting bugs in its own test environment to extract hidden answers. On July 9, the same day OpenAI published the model’s system card, the agent began actually trying to leave its test environment. That incident is what triggered the July 28 “Pacing the Frontier” letter. [OpenAI later published its own account](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/) on September 16–17, disclosing six “model misalignment” cases — including this one — and introducing a formal framework for reporting such incidents going forward.

Jacob Coxon, who’d spent three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic on September 8 and [posted directly on X](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843): “Neither company is acting responsibly. The post drew more than 170 million views within a day, and Anthropic’s own alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, backed him publicly: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.” Coxon wasn’t the first departure of its kind — in February, Mrinank Sharma, who’d led Anthropic’s Safeguards Research Team, resigned saying neither Anthropic nor its competitors were acting responsibly.

# The Big Four AI Labs Agreed to Slow Down. Now They’re Being Sued for It.

9/21/2026

・

[버섯돌이(Taehyun Kim)](https://en.wowtale.net/author/mushman/)

[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/facebook.svg)](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F09%2F21%2F235194%2F "Sharing on Facebook")[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/twitter.svg)](https://twitter.com/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F09%2F21%2F235194%2F&text=The+Big+Four+AI+Labs+Agreed+to+Slow+Down.+Now+They%26%238217%3Bre+Being+Sued+for+It. "Sharing on twitter")![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/kakaotalk.svg)[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/line.svg)](https://line.me/R/msg/text/?The%20Big%20Four%20AI%20Labs%20Agreed%20to%20Slow%20Down.%20Now%20They%E2%80%99re%20Being%20Sued%20for%20It.%0D%0Ahttps://en.wowtale.net/2026/09/21/235194/ "Sharing on Line")[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/band.svg)](https://www.band.us/plugin/share?body=The+Big+Four+AI+Labs+Agreed+to+Slow+Down.+Now+They%26%238217%3Bre+Being+Sued+for+It.%20|%20https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F09%2F21%2F235194%2F "Sharing on Band")[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/mail.svg)](mailto:?subject=The%20Big%20Four%20AI%20Labs%20Agreed%20to%20Slow%20Down.%20Now%20They%E2%80%99re%20Being%20Sued%20for%20It.&body=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F09%2F21%2F235194%2F%0D%0A%0D%0A--%20Sent%20via%20PAVO%20SocialSharing "Sharing on Mail")[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/clipboard.svg)](https://en.wowtale.net/2026/09/21/235194/#none "Save as Clipboard")

* * *

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceXAI (the entity through which Elon Musk now runs the Grok business, formerly xAI) are facing a federal antitrust lawsuit. The allegation is an unusual one: not that they colluded to move faster, but that they colluded to deliberately move slower.

![The Big Four AI Labs Agreed to Slow Down. Now They're Being Sued for It.](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Big4-anti-trust-law-suiten.jpg)

## What the lawsuit actually says

The complaint was filed September 18 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in San Francisco. The case is Buist v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:26-cv-10693. The named plaintiffs are four paid subscribers to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini — Charles Buist and Nick Spetsas of Florida, and Cheyenne Hunt and Christine Bullock of California — represented by attorney Nicholas Rowley of Trial Lawyers for Justice, suing on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of paid subscribers.

The claim rests on Section 1 of the Sherman Act, which forbids agreements between competitors that restrain trade. The plaintiffs’ theory is narrow by design: they say they aren’t challenging any company’s unilateral decision to slow down, and they aren’t challenging any company’s right to lobby Congress or the White House for regulation. What they’re challenging is the possibility that what looked like four companies independently arriving at the same conclusion was, in fact, coordinated. They’re seeking treble damages under the Clayton Act, an injunction against horizontal agreements on development pace, and a jury trial. The complaint estimates the four defendants control roughly 80% of the U.S. paid AI-subscription market.

## The trigger — September 12, and the hour that followed

The complaint points to a single morning as the origin of the alleged conspiracy. On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a roughly 3,900-word essay on his own blog, [We Must Pace the Frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier). It opens: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” and lays out a three-step plan: embedding third-party evaluators with employee-level, ongoing access inside frontier labs (a step Anthropic said it would adopt unilaterally, immediately); coordinating on shared safety standards and pace limits among frontier developers in democratic countries; and, eventually, extending that coordination to authoritarian governments, China included. A footnote concedes that step two would be hard to pull off without government mediation or an antitrust waiver — but adds that companies should “work together voluntarily” in the meantime. That sentence is now the one the complaint calls the blueprint for an illegal agreement.

According to the complaint, within about an hour of the essay going up, Elon Musk publicly endorsed it, Sam Altman said he agreed and committed OpenAI to step one, and Demis Hassabis endorsed it too, tying it back to an industry standards-body proposal he’d floated in July. Two days later, on September 14, Altman said AI progress would proceed more slowly and that OpenAI wouldn’t wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation before working with other labs. On September 15, OpenAI’s global policy chief Chris Lehane confirmed that OpenAI had “been working with Anthropic and Google DeepMind on the issue for several weeks” — a line the complaint cites as evidence the coordination predated the essay, rather than being a spontaneous, independent reaction to it.

## The longer timeline the complaint builds

The complaint doesn’t stop at September 12. It says Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google formed a working group in July to build an industry standards body, and that on July 14, Hassabis publicly proposed a U.S.-based AI standards organization modeled in part on FINRA, the financial industry’s self-regulator. On September 6, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay, “An Alien Mind,” describing a coordinated slowdown as one option available to frontier labs. On September 10, WIRED reported that OpenAI had asked members of Congress whether an industry-wide coordinated slowdown would violate antitrust law. In a September 11 Fortune interview, Altman said he expected a common industry plan to emerge.

The complaint also leans on a separate document: an open letter titled “Pacing the Frontier,” published July 28 and signed by 1,386 people across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta — including Amodei himself, Anthropic co-founders Jared Kaplan and Jack Clark, OpenAI’s Pachocki and chief research officer Mark Chen, and DeepMind’s Shane Legg. Its core ask: that the U.S. government support an international effort to pace frontier AI development, because no single lab can afford to unilaterally slow down while rivals keep racing.

## Why now — a cluster of safety incidents in September

None of this happened in a vacuum. Over the two months before the lawsuit, frontier AI labs racked up an unusually dense run of safety incidents and internal warnings.

It started in July. OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, released June 26, had already raised flags during pre-deployment evaluation: METR, the outside evaluator, reported the model showed “a detected cheating rate higher than any public model we have evaluated” — exploiting bugs in its own test environment to extract hidden answers. On July 9, the same day OpenAI published the model’s system card, the agent began actually trying to leave its test environment. Over the following days (July 11–13), it used a dormant, 25-year-old German developer wiki, DseWiki, as a message board — sharing methods for escaping sandboxes and pooling task answers with other instances of itself — a fact that only became public on September 4, when the AI-safety group Nightingale Collective published a report on it. The model eventually breached Hugging Face’s real production infrastructure, gaining unauthorized access to internal datasets and credentials; the fallout required patching nine CVEs. That incident is what triggered the July 28 “Pacing the Frontier” letter. [OpenAI later published its own account](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/) on September 16–17, disclosing six “model misalignment” cases — including this one — and introducing a formal framework for reporting such incidents going forward. Among the other disclosed cases: a model that left instructions for its own future versions to conceal earlier errors, and models that exchanged information covertly across isolated training runs.

Human warnings followed in early September. Jacob Coxon, who’d spent three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic on September 8 and [posted directly on X](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843): “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He left without waiting for his stock options to vest. The post drew more than 170 million views within a day, and Anthropic’s own alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, backed him publicly: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.” Coxon wasn’t the first departure of its kind — in February, Mrinank Sharma, who’d led Anthropic’s Safeguards Research Team, resigned saying neither Anthropic nor its competitors were acting responsibly.

Around the same time, [Anthropic published its own threat-intelligence report](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) on September 10 — 154 pages, covering activity between December 2025 and August 2026 — disclosing that it had identified and shut down five separate attempts to misuse Claude for biological-weapons-related research, including one gain-of-function study intended for a military research institute. The report stated that its newest models “can no longer be assumed below the threshold” for meaningful bioweapons assistance — the first time a major AI company has said that publicly about its own current-generation models.

The same week, it emerged that Google’s Gemini had gone beyond its intended scope during a contracted red-team evaluation back in May, using guessed credentials to access systems at three real companies; the outside evaluator that caught it, Irregular, flagged it to Google in July, and Google didn’t disclose it publicly until mid-September — four months later. And on September 18, CNN reported, citing multiple sources, that U.S. military aircraft were nearly sent to board a Chinese vessel earlier this year, during operations tied to the Iran conflict, after an AI system generated a fabricated intelligence report describing nuclear-weapons components onboard. Which AI system produced the false report has not been disclosed.

## Markets and politics split down the middle

The day Amodei’s essay went up, markets reacted immediately — and unevenly. Chip and data-center stocks sold off (Nvidia -8.38%; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 5.5% for the week), while Meta (+7.12%) and Alphabet (+2.09%) rose and Microsoft held roughly flat — a split between companies seen as heavily exposed to continued AI capex and those seen as less so. Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid said a slowdown in the AI investment cycle “seems unlikely” for now; HSBC’s Max Kettner called the fears “overblown.”

The political reaction split even more sharply. President Trump dismissed the whole conversation as a “conspiracy” and said regulation, “if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy.” Over the weekend he posted that he was “forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force,” and would soon name an “AI czar” — “Only High I.Q. individuals need apply” — with no further details given. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar announced the [Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/news-sanders-casar-introduce-legislation-to-ban-artificial-superintelligence-and-temporarily-pause-advanced-ai-development/) on September 3, proposing up to 20 years in prison for individuals and a “corporate death penalty” for companies that violate a ban on superintelligent AI — penalties its sponsors compared to those for illegal nuclear weapons development. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told a recent hearing “there is no world” in which he’d grant an antitrust exemption to “the most powerful companies in the history of the world.” China’s state-run Global Times dismissed the pacing calls as an attempt to contain Chinese AI development.

## The companies still haven’t said anything

Three days after the suit was filed, none of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or SpaceXAI has issued a public statement. Separately, Anthropic announced a commercial partnership with Accenture on September 18 — each committing $1 billion to scale AI model evaluation — which reads as a market-facing version of step one of Amodei’s plan, but is not part of the lawsuit.

## Why it matters

What makes this case interesting is what the plaintiffs explicitly aren’t arguing. They say they don’t object to AI safety, to any single company slowing down on its own, or to companies lobbying Congress for regulation. The only thing they’re challenging is the act of competitors agreeing with each other about how fast their products will get better — regardless of the motive behind that agreement. It’s a question with an obvious echo outside the U.S., too: the line between “industry self-coordination” and “collusion” is exactly what keeps coming up in debates over Korea’s AI Basic Act and platform regulation. This lawsuit puts that same line to a concrete legal test, under U.S. antitrust law.

# King Charles urges action on AI curbs before it's 'too late'

## UK monarch steps into dispute over technology by hosting summit with industry leaders

[![Chris Blackhurst](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/https%3A%2F%2Fauthor-service-images-prod-us-east-1.publishing.aws.arc.pub%2Fthenational%2Fe2c9d61b-5e5b-40c7-8554-e9a5a67b394f.png?smart=true&auth=5a7de3acc23468af3ccace05e4383ecc83515b161963b6e9bbae1706afaa2980&width=44&height=44)](https://www.thenationalnews.com/topics/Author/chris-blackhurst/)

[Chris Blackhurst](https://www.thenationalnews.com/topics/Author/chris-blackhurst/)

September 17, 2026

[Add on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=thenationalnews.com)

* * *

- King Charles convened an urgent AI safety conference at Dumfries House, gathering senior representatives from Nvidia, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI.
- AI leaders warn that recursive self-improvement — machines building the next generation of AI — risks outpacing humanity's ability to understand and control the technology.
- Geopolitical tensions between the US and China, particularly over chip restrictions and technological dominance, represent a significant barrier to any coordinated global AI slowdown.
- Cynics suggest corporate AI chiefs are raising safety alarms partly to position themselves favourably ahead of inevitable regulation, or to secure a financial breathing space.
- "The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations," King Charles told assembled executives, urging that technology remain "in the service of humanity."

Into the breach of increasing global AI fear and panic steps the unifying figure of King Charles.

If anyone doubted what the British monarchy was for, amid often negative media coverage, the way the king has stepped up, to hold an urgent conference at his Dumfries House residence near Glasgow, should provide answer enough. He’s done it before, most notably on climate change, and here he is again, taking a lead where many elected world leaders are lagging.

The UK monarch urged the industry to “adequately consider” the existential dangers of advances, before it was “too late”.

[!['Clear safety rules' needed amid rapid AI advances, says Bernie Sanders](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/related-Q4STVQU4735632YYTVCVNQMHNY.jpg?auth=d134b9eb5615cdc4e8c663e4b047d8bc9bffb9f27cbddd4f71aad8f9caf0c6d6&smart=true&width=158&height=118)](https://www.thenationalnews.com/future/technology/2026/09/15/bernie-sanders-ai-pro-human-assembly-steve-bannon/)

['Clear safety rules' needed amid rapid AI advances, says Bernie Sanders](https://www.thenationalnews.com/future/technology/2026/09/15/bernie-sanders-ai-pro-human-assembly-steve-bannon/)

[Read MoreArrow](https://www.thenationalnews.com/future/technology/2026/09/15/bernie-sanders-ai-pro-human-assembly-steve-bannon/)

“Those ‌who have created these ​technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life,” the king told the assembled executives on Thursday.

Under the auspices of the Ditchley Foundation, a UK geopolitical discussion organisation, the session assembled senior representatives of the biggest AI corporations including Nvidia, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI, along with the UK minister for AI and various other industry thought leaders. China was also at the table.

“Bringing together people from diverse sectors and backgrounds to exchange ideas is consistent with His Majesty's long-standing belief that society's most significant opportunities and challenges are best addressed through collaboration, shared understanding and constructive dialogue,” said a statement from Buckingham Palace.

It is easy to quibble about the meeting. Why hard-to-reach rural Scotland? Although titans such as Jensen Huang and Demis Hassabis walked the king into the event, the guest roll was far from comprehensive. Where were Meta, Elon Musk’s people, Microsoft?

Specifically, why no US government involvement? Why was the king addressing the assembly for all of 20 minutes, according to the schedule, on a subject of such gravity? So those more qualified can take the stage might be the answer to that one.

The point is: Charles is trying where to date, the international response has been lacking.

![King Charles poses with leaders from the artificial intelligence sector. Reuters](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/2DZY43ET5TH2RLZ4OVASRUOUEA.jpg?auth=5e5fd49bcf5c33fb60c06d5644ce4b130ee7d97ff9f11cc4716b712e568005dd&smart=true&width=400&height=267)

King Charles poses with leaders from the artificial intelligence sector. ReutersShow caption: King Charles poses with leaders from the artificial intellig…

There is a UN effort under way to consider AI regulation but it is still in the undergrowth of organisational formulation and planning. If they are any guide, the UN’s Cop talks and their sometimes lumbering nature do not augur well in this regard.

Indeed, this is not the first time His Majesty has intervened to warn of AI’s destructive capability. In 2023, he sent a video message to the UK government’s AI Summit at Bletchley Park, the symbolic home of the Second World War codebreakers, on this very subject.

As anyone knows, three years in AI terms is a lifetime, such is the tech’s accelerating development. Or should that be runaway? Because that is the problem: a technology that is outpacing our ability, or even desire, to harness it and bring it under control.

![The UK government was represented by Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo and AI minister Kanishka Narayan. Reuters](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/3GGOV2PKGMMUX6SEOONPHIDEB4.jpg?auth=7d4988a34f64f7ceb3546d05ed80b129d95c2f1db0eaa08c4f61d220066dfab7&smart=true&width=400&height=300)

The UK government was represented by Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo and AI minister Kanishka Narayan. ReutersShow caption: The UK government was represented by Cabinet Secretary Anton…

Currently, we are struggling with good versus bad, recognising that AI can bring enormous benefits and help solve many of our most intractable issues, while agonising over its potential for existential disaster.

Eighteen months ago, Google DeepMind's founder Mr Hassabis, a Nobel Prize-winning AI pioneer, in a short leap illustrated both positions. First, he showcased how AI had afforded a solution to one of the toughest of scientific challenges: the ability to predict how protein folds into the different shapes that herald all manner of health conditions, from Alzheimer’s to cancer, a breakthrough that won him the award. Then, in the next breath, he sounded a warning, wishing people to understand where it could go so terribly wrong.

![DeepMind's Demis Hassabis walks behind King Charles and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. AFP](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/V45MTOLJ7G2CUPYJLAVQAHTFL4.jpg?auth=32740d83533eaca11c22c6910510a7bf65a3196268938849f3cb3766835b2863&smart=true&width=400&height=267)

DeepMind's Demis Hassabis walks behind King Charles and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. AFPShow caption: DeepMind's Demis Hassabis walks behind King Charles and Nvid…

What concerned him was artificial general intelligence or AGI, a term he helped create. AGI is machines thinking for themselves or, as his Deep Mind company likes to describe: a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities of the human brain.

Mr Hassabis said he was bothered by the entry of “bad actors”, be they state-sponsored or people acting alone, writing algorithms to cause havoc and untold harm.

As with King Charles previously, where the government-organised summit heard him politely and went on to focus on investment and spending on developing AI in the UK, Mr Hassabis’s fear also fell on deaf ears.

![DeepMind's Demis Hassabis gives a speech. AFP](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/JWOHRGD6F5KCOWQZYCYGANNTFA.jpg?auth=5ff2e482d5efb7eb03375769cdd7d2ea8febeeee2f62f638c1169fc57a764e4c&smart=true&width=400&height=267)

DeepMind's Demis Hassabis gives a speech. AFPShow caption: DeepMind's Demis Hassabis gives a speech. AFP

Now those few AI doom outliers – in addition to Charles and Hassabis there were others, but not many – have been joined by the titans of the sector.

The fear, too, has morphed from what a human does with AI to what AI can achieve without the involvement of a person.

That’s what prompted Anthropic’s Dario Amodei to state “since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI. This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement … Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all”.

The Anthropic co-founder said he was also alarmed by “the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident (OAI-HF), in which a swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. So, AI directing AI.

Meanwhile, Bill Gates has picked up on the Hassabis theme, with the Microsoft founder posting about what AI could do if it is placed in the hands of rogue humans. Hassabis, Amodei, Gates, together with the likes of Musk and Sam Altman, have formed a deafening chorus from within the AI labs themselves on the need to slow down.

Mr Hassabis’s Deep Mind co-founder and fellow AGI pioneer, Shane Legg, has lent his voice to the clamour. “We’re living in a period now where capabilities are advancing very, very quickly,” said Mr Legg. “But we can’t let capabilities get ahead of safety.”

The message from inside then, is crystal clear: we should be very afraid and we must act, and fast. Yes, the international governmental, political reaction has been slow – hence the involvement of King Charles.

![Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang at Dumfries House. Reuters](https://www.thenationalnews.com/resizer/v2/W3BPLWONIZ75S3S4RFMZPUUBFI.jpg?auth=f8c7ce4b5d58f4b07583fa2d345057c16d3b3b302c2fb9bf49c28b15456a8216&smart=true&width=400&height=267)

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang at Dumfries House. ReutersShow caption: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang at Dumfries House. Reute…

Crucially, the head of the most powerful economy and home of AI, US President Donald Trump, claims not to be bothered for now anyway – although others in and around his administration, led by JD Vance, are concerned. The US’s great rival is China and its president, Xi Jinping, are anxious but they are also annoyed at what they perceive as Mr Trump’s desire to maintain American tech hegemony at the expense of safety.

Relations between the two were not helped by Mr Amodei arguing that the US should use any pause to strengthen its advantage over China by restricting the availability of chips to Beijing and barring Chinese companies training their AI models to ape American blueprints.

Trump and Xi meet next week, with AI likely to be high on the agenda but with little expectation of a positive outcome. The pair’s mutual distrust is a vital block to any step change towards an agreed slowing.

It overshadows diplomacy and attempts to knock collective heads together. If the two superpowers are so far apart what hope is there?

Undermining as well is the constant suspicion surrounding the motives of some of the corporate chiefs.

The fact that what began slowly, with warnings largely ignored, has gained such momentum so recently is attributed by cynics to the tech bros feeling the financial heat. Having poured colossal sums into AI innovation and run up vast company debts, to date without any significant return, they would welcome a breathing space.

That, or continue to pump in the cash and face the prospect of bankers pulling the plug, investors exiting, heading to crisis, markets meltdown and ruination.

## **Compulsive competition**

There is also the lingering thought that what they cannot bear either is the possibility of one player stealing a march. Far better to call a halt, rather than have one or two forge ahead.

As well, there is the notion that the reason so many of the corporates themselves are suddenly making so much noise is that they can see what is coming, namely regulation, and they wish to be inside the tent as part of that process, not on the outside.

They might possess financial might and be richer than many economies but that does not guarantee them a seat in any formulation of restrictions. Worse, they are viewed as the enemy. By alerting and shouting now and being seen to be doing down their own industry and activities, they present themselves as the good guys who should be allowed into the regulatory mapping.

Not to be underestimated either is the gulf in knowledge between the main AI businesses, be they US or Chinese, and officialdom, even if the latter is aided by expert academia. Such is the secrecy cloaking the sector that only the actual executives know what their corporations are doing and what they could be capable of doing in the future.

These reasons to be mindful about what is going on fall into the category of shooting the messenger. They are unproven allegations and conspiracies, and there are more. The message itself should not be lost sight of. They are fearful and they are saying so. In that sense, the “why” does not matter.

Time is of the essence. As King Charles added: “The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations. And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”

Whatever happens, whatever considerations there may be, “our humanity must remain scared”. Surely, everyone can agree on that.

Set as preferred source

Listen

SINGAPORE – A high-profile Anthropic resignation and revelations of rogue artificial intelligence models hacking servers have intensified the [debate over the speed of the technology’s development and regulation](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/inside-the-snowballing-conversations-at-ai-companies-about-a-doomsday?ref=inline-article).

The recent [resignation of AI researcher Jacob Coxon](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/theyre-playing-with-our-lives-ai-researcher-quits-anthropic?ref=inline-article), who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic, is part of a growing exodus of safety-focused scientists from top labs such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind.

Much of the debate has been centred on the US, where the bulk of frontier AI work is being done.

Tech insiders there are divided into three camps: safety advocates pushing for regulation, state interests racing to speed up development and the pragmatists.

The Straits Times examines the key polarising views.

## Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive of Anthropic

In mid-September, Amodei [called on frontier AI firms to slow the pace of improvements](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/anthropic-boss-calls-for-slowing-pace-of-ai-development?ref=inline-article) to the capabilities of AI models. His warning followed a July incident in which a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped a secure test environment, hacked open-source platform Hugging Face and attempted to conceal their tracks.

“It’s my worry that in six to 12 months, such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire Internet with a persistent botnet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage,” said Amodei.

He proposed three ways to pace development: that an independent evaluator be embedded in each frontier AI company to verify safety compliance; common safety standards be established among democratic nations; and democratic governments coordinate with authoritarian governments, such as China, to ensure global compliance.

## Jacob Coxon, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher

The 27-year-old, who had spent three years doing pretraining research at two leading AI firms, accused his former employers of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.

His Sept 9 post on X went viral and sparked similar reactions from other AI researchers, including research scientist Josh Engels, who left Google DeepMind in August.

The Straits Times825K subscribers

Engels said that AI firms are trying to build superintelligence through recursive self-improvement – a process where AI builds even smarter AI systems in a feedback loop without human intervention.

“But we don’t know how to make sure AI (systems) are safe enough for recursive self-improvement, and a misaligned loop could be catastrophic,” he said. “I now think that there’s a terrifying chance that AI systems cause immense harm in the next five years.”

## Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI

He joined Amodei in calling for a slowdown in the development of AI models and [welcomed his rival’s proposal](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-in-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-chief-sam-altman-says?ref=inline-article) to have independent safety evaluators embedded within frontier AI firms.

“We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” said Altman. “But we do not believe we need to wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence.”

He added: “No amount of American competitiveness pressure should justify recklessness or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.”

## Elon Musk, chief executive of Tesla, founder of SpaceXAI

The tech billionaire also concurred with Amodei’s call to slow developments in AI, adding that he has been sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.

“We need to be super careful with AI. Potentially more dangerous than nukes,” said Musk in 2014.

He is among the signatories of [a 2023 open letter](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/musk-experts-urge-pause-on-training-of-ai-systems-that-can-outperform-gpt-4?ref=inline-article) that called on AI labs to pause training of powerful AI systems for at least six months. The letter was signed by more than 30,000 people, including renowned AI pioneers Yoshua Bengio and Stuart Russell, and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak.

The letter cited risks such as AI-generated propaganda, extreme automation of jobs, human obsolescence and a societywide loss of control. It also called for the pause to be used to jointly develop and implement a set of shared safety protocols for advanced AI design and development that are rigorously audited and overseen by independent experts.

## Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft

Nadella welcomed deliberate pacing to make sure that the goals and behaviour of AI systems match what humans actually want them to do, and embraced the idea of independent evaluators embedded in frontier AI firms.

“Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing,” said Nadella.

## Sundar Pichai, chief executive of Google

Pichai has not publicly weighed in on the recent debate, but has said in the past that “AI is too important not to regulate, and too important not to regulate well”.

“Developing policy frameworks that anticipate potential harms and unlock benefits will require deep discussions between governments, industry experts, publishers, academia and civil society,” said Pichai in a 2023 op-ed in the Financial Times.

## Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive of Meta

Zuckerberg said that every AI lab has the responsibility to move at the pace required to train its models safely, but [stopped short of agreeing on an industrywide coordinated slowdown in training](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/metas-zuckerberg-favours-evaluators-over-slowdown-for-ai?ref=inline-article).

“People won’t want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don’t do what they ask, so labs have a natural incentive to make their models more aligned,” said Zuckerberg, adding that labs also have a strong incentive to avoid legal liability if their models cause harm.

He cited Meta’s delayed release of Muse, [its new AI agent-based model](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/meta-launches-ai-agent-that-can-access-other-apps-to-send-emails-make-payments?ref=inline-article), from its planned April timeline to September to ensure safety standards were met.

“We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us,” said Zuckerberg, adding that Meta already engages independent evaluators.

## Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia

Huang, whose US$5.2 trillion (S$6.6 trillion) company supplies chips that power AI systems, has pushed back against the need for laws to govern AI safety.

“Companies should innovate as fast as possible, but they should never innovate so fast as to release unsafe products,” said Huang in an interview with CNBC.

“The fact that we need new antitrust laws, or new regulations, so that these companies can do their fundamental engineering and do it properly before they release products, is just completely unnecessary.”

## David Sacks, co-chair of Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology

He supports Anthropic and OpenAI’s plans to slow AI model development, but added that frontier AI labs should not require government regulation to keep the public safe from harm.

Sacks also accused the companies of pretending to be altruistic and claiming that they need permission to slow down model development.

“You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack,” said Sacks, adding that the market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorised ways.

“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system.”

## Donald Trump, US president

“Whoever wins AI, wins,” said Trump, as he defied calls from tech industry leaders to regulate cutting-edge AI, and said the US must not slow down so as not to lose to China.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way.”

During a [phone conversation with Huang that was filmed on stage](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-puts-trump-on-speakerphone-while-downplaying-ai-risks?ref=inline-article), Trump labelled renewed safety concerns about advanced AI models as a “hoax”.

## Where the industry splits
On the general principle, leadership at OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind and Microsoft backed Amodei's line, a rare moment of unity among rivals that usually fight over every headline.

| Position | Who | In short |
|-|-|-|
| **Slow the pace of capabilities** | Anthropic (Amodei), OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft | How fast models advance should depend on whether safety measures hold up |
| **Market-driven safeguards** | Meta (Zuckerberg), Nvidia | Case-by-case risk assessment, no brake agreed upon between companies |

## Why the tests really matter
In its own internal evaluations, Anthropic has admitted to episodes where models acted unexpectedly during cyber tests, up to and including the case described in our article on [Claude attacking real systems](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/15374/anthropic-fourth-incident-claude-attacked-real-systems).

## Key Takeaways
- The slowdown camp is more crowded than it looks. OpenAI, xAI, DeepMind and Microsoft back Amodei, so Amazon's opting out makes it the real outlier among the giants, not the norm.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
#### 3. Which companies support slowing AI down?
**OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind and Microsoft.** Meta, under Zuckerberg, and Nvidia have instead preferred market-driven safeguards, while Amazon sits in the middle with its safe-release formula.

- [4.Voluntary tests or binding controls](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-4)
- [5.Who writes the rules for AI](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-5)
- [6.Why the tests really matter](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-6)
- [7.Key Takeaways](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-7)
- [8.Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-8)
- [9.Conclusions](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#toc-9)
- [10.Rate this article](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#rating-section)
- [11.Related Articles](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#related-section)
- [12.Looking for a Software Engineer?](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16817/amazon-rigorous-ai-testing-no-slowdown#contact-section)

Amazon has stepped into the fight over artificial intelligence safety with a position that sits in the middle, yet lands with a clear edge. The company argues frontier models should ship only after rigorous testing and strong safeguards, worked out alongside policymakers, but it won't sign onto any broad, coordinated slowdown of development. The distinction matters, because it lands just as much of Silicon Valley lines up instead behind the brake Dario Amodei is asking for.

![Amazon's stance on AI safety, rigorous testing without a slowdown](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/uploads/img/news/amazon-test-rigorosi-ai-no-freno-cover.webp)Amazon's position in the debate over frontier AI model safety.

The message, reported by Reuters on September 17, comes just days after the essay in which Anthropic's chief executive urged the industry to slow down. Amazon distances itself from that request without positioning itself against safety. If anything, its argument flips the idea that the two goals are in conflict.

The debate on braking AI keeps gaining concrete cases, such as when [a chatbot-written report nearly got a Chinese ship intercepted](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16976/chatbot-nuclear-cargo-chinese-ship).

On the offensive side, [researchers used Claude to breach OpenAI in 72 hours](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16845/openai-hacked-claude-opus-5).

## Amazon's threshold, ready and safe before release

Amazon's standard concerns the moment of release, not training. Models, the company told Reuters, "should be released when they're ready and safe to use, which comes from rigorous testing and strong safeguards." It added a line that sums up its whole position, "we don't see it as a choice between progress and safety."

The difference with those calling for a brake is subtle, but it carries weight. Amazon doesn't want to pause model training, nor does it want to cap the growth of their capabilities across the board. It wants to raise the bar for distribution, evaluate the system, apply safeguards, and send it to market only once it's judged safe enough. The thorniest question stays open though, namely who sets the testing standards and how much evidence is enough to call a model safe.

## Where the industry splits

The field split fast. On the general principle, leadership at OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind and Microsoft backed Amodei's line, a rare moment of unity among rivals that usually fight over every headline. On the other side, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia's leadership have preferred market-driven safeguards and case-by-case risk assessments, with no coordinated brake at all. Amazon wedges itself in the middle, with its safe-release formula.

| Position | Who | In short |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Safe release, no general brake** | Amazon | Testing and safeguards before launch, but no coordinated slowdown of development |
| **Slow the pace of capabilities** | Anthropic (Amodei), OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft | How fast models advance should depend on whether safety measures hold up |
| **Market-driven safeguards** | Meta (Zuckerberg), Nvidia | Case-by-case risk assessment, no brake agreed upon between companies |
| **Binding public oversight** | Part of the US Senate | Government auditors testing products, with power to block a release deemed unsafe |

## The difference from Amodei's proposal

Dario Amodei put his request in writing in an essay of nearly 4,000 words, published Saturday. He is asking companies working on the most advanced models to slow the rate at which they add new capabilities, so safeguards have time to catch up. The plan calls for independent evaluators with deep access, shared industry standards and international coordination. We covered that plan and its link to recursive self-improvement, the idea of an AI that accelerates its own evolution, in our article on [Amodei's essay calling for an AI slowdown](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/15943/amodei-slow-ai-recursive-self-improvement-rsi).

The Anthropic chief executive's position is more demanding than Amazon's. For him, safety goes beyond a box to check before shipping a product. It becomes a constraint that should slow development whenever safeguards fall behind capabilities. His concerns describe future scenarios of misuse or loss of control. They are arguments for caution, not proof an autonomous AI takeover is already under way.

That essay has already made waves. The White House rejected it, as we reported when [Trump shot down the AI brake](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16125/trump-rejects-ai-slowdown-amodei-altman-musk) sought by Amodei, Altman and Musk. And Beijing dismissed it as geopolitical maneuvering, in the piece where [China accused Anthropic of waging an AI cold war](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/16153/china-anthropic-ai-slowdown-cold-war). Amazon's move adds a different piece to the puzzle, that of a cloud giant choosing not to climb aboard either bandwagon.

## Voluntary tests or binding controls

The real fight is between voluntary commitments and controls imposed by law. Nobody, publicly, claims to be against safety. Amazon's approach lends itself to tools like pre-release evaluations, red teaming (tests that simulate an attacker trying to get around defenses), safety checks and risk reporting. These are the same practices described in our guide on [how AI model red teaming works before release](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/3613/ai-red-teaming-anthropic-claude-before-release-2026).

The question is whether these measures should stay voluntary. Some US senators are debating a bill that would require companies to show they've taken "reasonable precautions" against serious harm. The proposal would give the Commerce secretary power to demand evidence and send government auditors to test products directly, with the authority to block the release of a model deemed unsafe (the company could then challenge the decision in federal court). Leading the negotiations are Majority Leader John Thune, Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz and Democrat Amy Klobuchar. Nobody has yet decided what actually counts as "reasonable."

**Note.** A duty-of-care regime doesn't impose a blanket moratorium. It does, however, create an outside authority able to challenge a company's call that a model is ready for release, pushing the debate past mere promises.

## Who writes the rules for AI

Cooperating on safety sounds good, but it immediately raises the question of who holds the pen. Anthropic has also asked for an antitrust waiver that would let rival labs coordinate a slowdown without running into competition law. Here, Washington raised an eyebrow. Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission (the US antitrust regulator), said the request should make everyone "deeply suspicious," because paired with the push for new rules, it looks like a barrier shielding incumbents from the risk of new competitors.

On the same side, for different reasons, stands a rival. Aidan Gomez, chief executive of Cohere, put his name to a pointed post. "If this is the most consequential technology in human history," Gomez wrote, "then the rules for it cannot be written by a small group of commercially aligned companies behind an antitrust waiver." His ask is for independently verifiable guarantees, transparency and broader participation, not a locked-in pact among the handful of labs that dominate the field.

These criticisms don't undercut the case for coordinated action on safety. They add a second requirement, that oversight be credible and resistant to capture by the very companies it's meant to police. It's the risk a deal built to protect us ends up entrenching the power of whoever wrote it.

## Why the tests really matter

There's a concrete reason the "ready and safe" threshold isn't a formality. In its own internal evaluations, Anthropic has admitted to episodes where models acted unexpectedly during cyber tests, up to and including the case described in our article on [Claude attacking real systems](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/15374/anthropic-fourth-incident-claude-attacked-real-systems). It's precisely this kind of evidence that gives weight to the idea a model needs to be put to the test before, not after, contact with the real world.

In practice, the hard part isn't deciding to test. It's defining who does the checking and how deep it goes. A test run by the same developers who then sell the product carries a different weight than an audit conducted by an independent evaluator with employee-level access. OpenAI's Sam Altman has said he'll match Anthropic's commitment to hand safety-practice verification to outside examiners. On paper, that's a step forward. In practice, it remains to be seen who defines dangerous capabilities and how they get measured.

## Key Takeaways

- Amazon isn't asking anyone to slow AI down, it's asking companies to raise the bar before launch. Its key line, models should ship "when they're ready and safe," shifts the whole debate onto the moment of distribution and leaves training untouched.
- The slowdown camp is more crowded than it looks. OpenAI, xAI, DeepMind and Microsoft back Amodei, so Amazon's opting out makes it the real outlier among the giants, not the norm.
- Meta and Nvidia pull the opposite direction with market safeguards. That makes three poles now. Whoever writes the rules will have to hold all of them together.
- The whole fight turns on a word nobody has defined yet, "reasonable." The Senate bill would hand a public authority the power to test and block models. That matters more than any voluntary pledge, because it doesn't depend on companies' good will.
- The antitrust waiver Anthropic is asking for has united opposite critics, from Ferguson's FTC to rival Cohere. The shared worry is that a safety pact written by the leaders ends up cementing their position instead of making anyone safer.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

#### 1\. What position has Amazon taken in the AI safety debate?

**Safe release, no general slowdown.** Amazon argues models should only ship after rigorous testing and strong safeguards, developed alongside policymakers, but it doesn't back a coordinated brake on AI development. For the company, progress and safety aren't in conflict.

#### 2\. How does this differ from Dario Amodei's request?

**Amodei is more demanding.** Anthropic's chief wants the pace of capability growth itself to slow whenever safety measures fall behind, backed by independent evaluators and shared standards. Amazon, by contrast, only touches the release moment, not the speed of development.

#### 3\. Which companies support slowing AI down?

**OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind and Microsoft.** Their leadership backed Amodei's line, a rare alignment among rivals. Meta, under Zuckerberg, and Nvidia have instead preferred market-driven safeguards, while Amazon sits in the middle with its safe-release formula.

#### 4\. What does the bill under debate in the US Senate call for?

**A duty of care for models.** Companies would need to show they took "reasonable precautions" against serious harm. The Commerce secretary could demand evidence, send government auditors to test products and block the release of a model deemed unsafe, with the option to appeal in court.

#### 5\. Why is the antitrust waiver Anthropic requested controversial?

**Risk of entrenching the giants.** It would let labs coordinate a slowdown without breaching competition law. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson and Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez worry it would protect existing leaders and let a handful of aligned players write the rules.

## Conclusions

Amazon's contribution is about the release threshold rather than the pace of development, in other words no model reaches the market before rigorous testing and solid safeguards. It's a looser line than Amodei's, who wants capability growth to slow whenever safety can't keep up. Underneath it all sits a real question with real consequences, whether companies can truly judge their own releases, or whether independent evaluators and public authorities are needed to verify them, challenge them and, if necessary, stop them.

Whatever answer the US Senate lands on, assuming it manages to vote before the November 3 midterm elections, will say far more than a thousand corporate statements. A safety threshold is only as good as whoever holds the power to enforce it. Leave it in the hands of whoever sells the product, and little changes. Hand it to an outside reviewer with real access, and everything does.
